newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ukraine worried about potential nuclear neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine worried about potential nuclear neighbours.

text.p: Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennadi Udovenko expressed concern on Thursday at the possible deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of some of his country's neighbours -- an allusion to their potential membership in NATO.

In a speech to the General Assembly, he said a proposal by Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma for the establishment of a nuclear weapon-free zone in Central and Eastern Europe between the Baltic and Black Seas was the next logical step in the process of nuclear disarmament.
"I would like to emphasise that the possible deployment of nuclear weapons on the territories of our neighbours in Central and Eastern Europe is a matter of great concern to us," Udovenko said.
He did not mention by name Poland, Hungary or the Czech Republic, widely regarded as potential NATO members.

Udovenko told the Assembly: "We believe that support of the idea of a non-nuclear Central Europe would promote an atmosphere of confidence between and among the states of the region and would prevent the emergence of new dividing lines on the European continent."

Such a zone in the centre of Europe, in addition to existing nuclear-free zones in Antarctica, the South Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean as well as in Southern and in Southern and Eastern Asia and Africa "will create the 'critical mass' which would foster the process of nuclear disarmament," he said.

Ukraine had been a nuclear weapons-free state since June 1, "having eliminated the world's third largest nuclear arsenal, one which we inherited," Udovenko said, referring to weapons dating from the Soviet era.

"We believe that by having done this, Ukraine has made an unprecedented contribution, which has not yet received adequate recognition by the international community, to diminishing the global threat and thus demonstrated to the whole world its peaceful, consistent and predictable policy."
Udovenko said he he would sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty on Friday, which bans all nuclear weapons explosions.

The accord, opened for signature on Tuesday, has so far been subscribed by more than 70 countries, including the five declared nuclear weapons powers -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France.

Udovenko said Ukraine's strategic aim was integration into European and Euro-Atlantic structures while its continuing committment to non-bloc status was proved by having become on Wednesday an observer in the non-aligned movement.
